patterns.pattern: Moved instead of stopped
patterns.role: Sent abusers away and received them
patterns.role_note: Orán → Vatican: Bishop Gustavo Zanchetta; Verona → Mendoza: Fr Nicola Corradi.
patterns.pattern_summary: When a priest, religious brother, teacher or head teacher was found to be abusing children, the institution they worked for often moved them instead of reporting them to the police. The move was to another parish, another school, another state or another country, and the person went on working with children. A Pennsylvania grand jury reported in 2018 that bishops in six dioceses had moved priests they knew to be abusers. In Australia, Bishop Mulkearns knew by late 1975 that the priest Gerald Ridsdale was abusing children and kept appointing him to new parishes. In Melbourne in 2008, the Adass Israel School paid for its head teacher, Malka Leifer, to fly to Israel before the police were told of the allegations against her. In England, an internal report in 1982 described how the barrister John Smyth had beaten boys he met through evangelical holiday camps; he moved to Zimbabwe in 1984, the police were not told until 2013, and a 2024 review called him "a problem solved and exported to Africa". The map draws 34 documented moves and colors the countries that sent or received an abuser.

patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role_note: 1984: CONADEP, Nunca Más (1984) — children kidnapped and born in captivity.
patterns.pattern_summary: Governments and churches held official inquiries into child abuse in institutions at different times. Canada's Hughes inquiry into the Mount Cashel orphanage began in 1989, and Ireland's Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse ran from 1999 to 2009. In the United States, Catholic bishops commissioned a national study that was published in 2004, and state grand juries and attorneys general followed. Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and Austria began inquiries after a wave of disclosures in 2010. Australia's Royal Commission sat from 2013 to 2017, the inquiry for England and Wales ran from 2014 to 2022, and New Zealand's from 2018 to 2024. France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland reported between 2021 and 2023. Several of these studies were commissioned and paid for by the Catholic Church itself. Where an inquiry surveyed the general population instead of relying on church records, the numbers were much higher: France's commission estimated that about 216,000 people had been abused as children by priests and members of religious orders since 1950, compared with about 3,000 cases the church had identified. In Italy the only national figures come from reports the Italian bishops' conference has published about itself since 2022. Brazil's Congress held inquiries into the sexual exploitation of children that reported in 2004, 2010 and 2014. The research for this map found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in the Philippines or India; India's official findings are state-level audits of children's homes, such as the 2018 audit of 110 homes in Bihar.

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role: Sending country, later closed or suspended
patterns.role_note: 2025: Argentina — Abuelas de Plaza de Mayo: 140 stolen grandchildren identified
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. patterns.pattern: Children taken by governments, then abused or given false identities
patterns.role: Dictatorship or occupation: children given to other families under false identities
patterns.role_note: Argentina — junta's 'systematic plan' to appropriate babies (2012 verdict). Argentina — Abuelas de Plaza de Mayo: 140 stolen grandchildren identified.
patterns.pattern_summary: In several countries the government itself took children from their parents, and the records show those children were then sexually abused or handed to other families under false identities. During Argentina's military dictatorship from 1976 to 1983, babies born to women held in secret detention were taken and given to military families and allies of the regime. In 2012 a Buenos Aires court found this had been a "systematic plan" and sentenced the former dictator Jorge Videla to 50 years. By July 2025 the Grandmothers of Plaza de Mayo had identified 140 of those children. Uruguay, Chile, El Salvador and Franco's Spain had similar cases, in which children were taken without their parents' consent and adopted by other families at home or abroad, often under changed names. Nazi Germany took children from occupied Poland and placed them with German families under new identities. In Canada and the United States, Indigenous children were sent to government-funded residential and boarding schools. Canada's Truth and Reconciliation Commission reported in 2015, and by the end of 2014 nearly 38,000 claims had been made for physical and sexual abuse at the schools. A US federal report in 2022 said many children at its 417 boarding schools suffered physical, sexual and emotional abuse. Britain sent children abroad to Australia, Canada and other countries under child migration schemes, and a 2018 inquiry found evidence that children sent under these schemes were sexually abused. In Ireland and South Korea, inquiries found that adoption agencies working with the state falsely registered children as orphans or hid their identities.

cases.title: Próvolo Institute, Luján de Cuyo (Mendoza) — convictions 2019
cases.who: Provolo Institute for the Deaf (Argentina branch); Fr Nicola Corradi, Fr Horacio Corbacho, gardener Armando Gómez; Sr Kumiko Kosaka charged
cases.what: Priests Nicola Corradi (Italian) and Horacio Corbacho and other staff of the Provolo school for deaf children in Luján de Cuyo, Mendoza were arrested in 2016, charged with abusing at least two dozen students. On 25 November 2019 a Mendoza court convicted Corradi, Corbacho and gardener Armando Gómez of abusing children at the school between 2004 and 2016; the victims in the trial were 10 former students. Corradi was sentenced to 42 years, Corbacho to 45 and Gómez to 18. Nun Kumiko Kosaka was charged in 2017 with helping the abuse and with physically abusing students.
cases.cover_up: Corradi had been accused in Verona in 2009 yet continued at the Argentine school; Japanese nun Kumiko Kosaka charged with abuse and covering up

cases.title: Argentina — junta's 'systematic plan' to appropriate babies (2012 verdict)
cases.who: Argentine military junta; armed forces and security forces; ESMA
cases.what: On 5 July 2012 Federal Oral Criminal Tribunal No. 6 of Buenos Aires found that the military junta had run a systematic plan to abduct children born to detained or disappeared mothers, between 1976 and 1983. Former dictator Jorge Videla was sentenced to 50 years and the last dictator, Reynaldo Bignone, to 15 years; nine other defendants received 15 to 40 years (MercoPress). The trial covered about 31–35 abductions. The tribunal convicted Bignone of crimes against humanity for implementing the plan.
cases.cover_up: Children's original identities were hidden and they were registered as the biological children of military families and regime allies.

cases.title: Wonderland Club / Operation Cathedral
cases.who: The Wonderland Club (encrypted online network)
cases.what: An international online ring that ran for about four years over encrypted internet chat; each new member had to supply 10,000 images of child abuse. Members held at least 750,000 images and 1,800 videos. Led by the UK National Crime Squad, police in 12 to 13 countries (reported figures differ) acted simultaneously on 2 September 1998, about 1,500 officers raiding 107 homes and making 104 arrests. CNN reported in February 2001 that only 17 of the children in the images had been identified, six of them in Britain. The investigation began after US Customs exposed a related ring, the Orchid Club, in 1996.

cases.title: Marita Verón case — Tucumán brothel network
cases.who: Brothel and trafficking ring in Tucumán province
cases.what: Marita Verón, aged 23, disappeared in Tucumán in 2002, allegedly abducted into forced prostitution. In December 2012 a Tucumán court acquitted all 13 defendants, provoking national protests and calls to impeach the judges. In December 2013 Tucumán's Supreme Court reversed the acquittals and found 10 of the 13 guilty. Her mother's foundation, created in 2008, says it has helped free hundreds of women and girls from brothels. (Verón was an adult; the case is included because it exposed the national network that also trafficked minors.)
cases.cover_up: Campaigners and the victim's family's lawyers said police were often paid to protect prostitution rings; trial court acquitted all 13 in 2012.

cases.title: Bishop Gustavo Zanchetta of Orán — convicted 2022
cases.who: Diocese of Orán; Bishop Gustavo Zanchetta
cases.what: Bishop Gustavo Zanchetta resigned from the Diocese of Orán in August 2017, citing health, after complaints from clergy, and in December 2017 Pope Francis gave him a post created for him at the Vatican's patrimony office (APSA). Clergy had complained to the nunciature in 2015–2016 about his behaviour with seminarians and explicit images on his phone. On 4 March 2022 a court in Salta sentenced him to four and a half years for continued sexual abuse of two former seminarians, aggravated by his being a minister of religion. Included as a case of a bishop moved to the Vatican, though the victims were adults.
cases.cover_up: After resigning in 2017 amid complaints he was given a post at the Vatican's APSA in December 2017; suspended in January 2019

cases.title: Uruguay — Gelman v. Uruguay: baby taken from disappeared mother (Operation Condor)
cases.who: Uruguayan Defense Information Service (SID); joint Argentine–Uruguayan commando under Operation Condor
cases.what: A pregnant 19-year-old Argentine detained in Buenos Aires in August 1976 was moved secretly to Montevideo, gave birth in a military hospital, and her baby was taken in December 1976 and left with a police officer's family, who raised her under another identity for 23 years. On 24 February 2011 the Inter-American Court of Human Rights found Uruguay responsible for enforced disappearance and suppression of the child's identity, and ruled the 1986 Expiry Law amnesty legally ineffective.
cases.cover_up: Uruguay's 1986 Expiry Law was used to close the investigation in 2003.

cases.title: Argentina — CONADEP 'Nunca Más': children of the disappeared taken and given to military families (1984)
cases.who: Argentine armed and security forces (1976–83)
cases.what: The National Commission on the Disappearance of Persons, created by President Raúl Alfonsín on 15 December 1983 and chaired by Ernesto Sábato, delivered its report Nunca Más on 20 September 1984. It recorded 8,960 forced disappearances between 1976 and 1983 and stated that no fewer than 200 children under 15 had been kidnapped; babies were taken with their parents or born to pregnant prisoners in detention camps and given to military families. The report was key evidence in the 1985 Trial of the Juntas.
cases.cover_up: Identities of children changed; records of births in detention not kept

cases.title: Argentina — Abuelas de Plaza de Mayo: 140 stolen grandchildren identified
cases.who: Argentine military regime (1976–83); military families and regime allies who received children
cases.what: The Grandmothers of Plaza de Mayo were founded in 1977 to find children kidnapped with their disappeared parents or born to mothers in detention, who were passed for adoption to military families and regime allies. Their work led to the creation of Argentina's National Bank of Genetic Data. On 7 July 2025 they announced the 140th grandchild identified: a man born on 17 April 1977 at the clandestine centre 'La Escuelita' in Bahía Blanca after his parents were kidnapped in Cutral Có, Neuquén. The Grandmothers had found 97 grandchildren by 2008 and 133 by July 2023.
cases.cover_up: Children were illegally adopted with their original identities hidden; many did not know they were adopted.

cases.title: Argentina raids on The Family (Children of God) communes
cases.who: The Family / Children of God
cases.what: On 1 September 1993 Judge Roberto Marquevich ordered raids on Family communes near Buenos Aires; 137 children were taken into state custody and about 30 members arrested. The judge said nine children showed signs of 'cruel and atrocious maltreatment', which the group disputed. Children were later released after examination and no convictions resulted. Raids in Australia (1992, including Panton Hill, Victoria), France and Spain also ended without convictions.

cases.title: Paraguay — Fr Carlos Urrutigoity and the removal of Bishop Livieres
cases.who: Diocese of Ciudad del Este
cases.what: Argentine priest Carlos Urrutigoity was accused in 2002 in the US of sleeping with boarding-school students, giving them alcohol and sexually abusing a recently graduated seminarian. He then moved to the Diocese of Ciudad del Este, Paraguay, and became its second-in-command in 2014. His case reportedly cost Bishop Livieres his post when Pope Francis removed him in 2014. He was moved back to Mendoza, Argentina, in June 2015. He has not been convicted.
cases.cover_up: After accusations in the US (a 2002 complaint over students at St Gregory's Academy in the Diocese of Scranton), he moved with his group to Ciudad del Este, where Bishop Rogelio Livieres made him vicar general in 2014. Pope Francis removed Livieres in 2014; Urrutigoity left in June 2015. La Nación reported at least five Argentine priests accused of abuse or crimes against humanity had sheltered in Paraguay.

networks.what: German sect enclave in Chile led by Paul Schäfer, convicted in 2006 of abusing 25 minors. Used by Pinochet's secret police DINA as a detention and torture site (Rettig Commission 1991). Germany's president acknowledged diplomatic failures in 2016.

networks.name: Roman Catholic Church
networks.what: The Holy See governs about 1.3 billion Catholics. From 1922 (and 1962) canonical abuse cases were handled under strict secrecy; from 2001 they were reserved to the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith under pontifical secret, which was lifted in December 2019. National inquiries in Ireland, the US, Australia, Germany, France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Portugal, Spain and elsewhere found bishops moved accused clergy and avoided police. The UN Committee on the Rights of the Child in 2014 found practices that led to impunity.

networks.name: The Family International (Children of God)
networks.what: Founded by David Berg. A UK High Court judge found in 1995 that the group, including top leaders, had sexually abused minors in the past, and ordered it to denounce Berg's writings.

patterns.pattern: Platforms, servers and the money behind them
patterns.role: Hosts the most reported abuse material (IWF 2025)
patterns.role_note: 87,959 web addresses actioned by the IWF in 2025 (28% of the total).
patterns.pattern_summary: Online abuse of children depends on ordinary businesses: companies that host websites, apps and social platforms, payment services and banks. The classified advertising site Backpage earned more than $500 million from advertisements, including ones used to sell children, before US authorities shut it down in 2018.

cases.title: Operation Blackwrist — Thai boys abused for Tor sites
cases.who: Tor site administrators in Thailand and Australia
cases.what: INTERPOL launched Operation Blackwrist in 2017 after finding, during routine dark web monitoring, material showing the abuse of 11 boys under 13, published weekly on a subscription website with nearly 63,000 users. Bulgaria's cybercrime police, supported by Europol, took down the servers; US HSI, New Zealand's Department of Internal Affairs, NCMEC and Australian police assisted. The main administrator in Thailand and a second administrator in Adelaide, Australia, were arrested in January 2018. In June 2018 a Thai court sentenced the Thai administrator to 146 years, and an associate received 36 years; on 17 May 2019 the Australian administrator was sentenced to 40 years and three months, the longest sentence ever imposed in Australia for child sex offences. INTERPOL said 50 children had been removed from harm and 9 offenders arrested in Thailand, Australia and the United States.

cases.title: Kidflix / Operation Stream
cases.who: Kidflix (paid streaming platform, 1.8 million users 2022–2025)
cases.what: Kidflix, created in 2021, let users stream as well as download abuse videos, paying in cryptocurrency converted to tokens; 91,000 unique videos (6,288 hours) were uploaded. German and Dutch authorities seized the server on 11 March 2025, when it held about 72,000 videos. Operation Stream, led by Bavarian police with 38 countries and Europol, identified 1,393 suspects and arrested 79 during action weeks in March 2025; Europol called it the largest child sexual exploitation operation in its history.

cases.title: Bulgaria — girls trafficked to Western Europe; exploitation in state institutions (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Traffickers; Roma forced marriages to third-country nationals
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers exploit Bulgarian women and girls in sex trafficking throughout Western Europe and in Sofia, resort areas and border towns, and cites a UN special rapporteur finding that child sexual exploitation, including potential sex trafficking, was prevalent among children in government-run institutions. Courts convicted 31 traffickers; only eight received custodial sentences.
cases.cover_up: Corruption in law enforcement and the judiciary and impunity for complicit officials were pervasive; 34 convicted traffickers received suspended sentences.

patterns.pattern: Years of waiting: protected by status
patterns.role_note: Mount Cashel Orphanage: first report 1975, first action 1989 (14 years). Royal Newfoundland Constabulary probe opened Dec 1975 was closed by the police chief nine days later; the Justice Department ordered the report rewritten (1976); Deputy Minister of Justice said further action unwarranted (1977) Graham James (hockey): first report 1996, first action 1997 (1 years). Received a federal pardon in 2007 that became public only in 2010

patterns.pattern: Deadlines, lobbying and bankruptcy
patterns.role_note: Ontario 2016: Bill 132 (Royal Assent 9 March 2016) removed limitation periods for civil claims based on sexual assault/abuse
patterns.pattern_summary: Most people abused as children do not tell anyone for many years. In many countries and US states the legal deadline for suing or prosecuting, called a statute of limitations, used to run out in a person's early twenties, before most had spoken. When legislatures proposed extending these deadlines or reopening old claims, the institutions that would face lawsuits lobbied against the changes. The Catholic Church spent about $10.6 million on lobbying in eight northeastern US states from 2011 to 2018. In Pennsylvania, which still has no window for old claims, the Pennsylvania Catholic Conference spent more than $7.6 million and the state's insurance federation nearly $20.7 million on lobbying from 2014 to 2024. These totals cover all the issues they lobbied on, not only this one. Where the deadlines were lifted anyway, many institutions filed for bankruptcy. From 2004 to 2025, 40 US Catholic dioceses and religious orders did so, several of them hours or days before a trial, a deposition or a new law took effect. The Boy Scouts of America and USA Gymnastics also filed.

patterns.pattern_summary: When a person accused of abusing a child is a soldier, a diplomat or a foreign citizen, whether they are tried depends on their own government. patterns.pattern: Travelling offenders: crack down here, it moves there
patterns.role: Offenders' home country: law to prosecute abroad
patterns.role_note: 1997: Canada: Criminal Code extraterritorial child sex tourism provisions (Bill C-27 in force 26 May 1997; Bill C-15A 23 July 2002); up to 14 years
patterns.pattern_summary: The records show offenders who travel abroad to abuse children moving to new places as old ones were policed. In the Philippines, the mayor of Manila closed the Ermita district in 1992, and many of its bars reopened in Angeles City, where the US Clark Air Base had closed the same year. Observers reported that child prostitution in Svay Pak, on the edge of Phnom Penh in Cambodia, grew after Thailand cracked down in the 1990s, and that when police raided Svay Pak in January 2003 the raid had been announced in advance and most of the children had been moved to Siem Reap and Sihanoukville. The countries the offenders came from passed laws allowing their citizens to be prosecuted for abusing children abroad: Germany in 1993, Australia in 1994, Canada in 1997, Japan in 1999 and the United States in 2003. Later the abuse moved online. In the Philippine cities where the charity International Justice Mission worked with police, the number of children sold in bars and on the street fell by 79 to 86 percent between 2006 and 2016. Between 2014 and 2017, the number of Philippine internet addresses used each month for the sexual exploitation of children rose more than twelvefold.

patterns.pattern: When spies, soldiers and police are named
patterns.role: Police ran abuse sites to catch users
patterns.role_note: Childs Play — run by Australia's Task Force Argos for 11 months (police ran abuse sites to catch users). Duplessis Orphans (Quebec) — healthy orphans falsely certified mentally ill and confined (claimed, not established).
patterns.pattern_summary: Claims that intelligence services run or protect networks that abuse children circulate widely. The records gathered for this map show a few cases where a state service was involved, several claims that investigations found to be false, and some that remain unproven. In Chile, Paul Schäfer, who founded the German settlement Colonia Dignidad in 1961, was convicted in 2006 of abusing children there; Chilean officials believe the Pinochet dictatorship used the settlement to torture its opponents, and Germany admitted in 2016 that its embassy had failed to act. In West Berlin, from the late 1960s, the city's youth authorities placed boys in foster care with men known to be paedophiles, on the advice of the psychologist Helmut Kentler. In Afghanistan, US soldiers were told not to intervene when Afghan commanders allied with them abused boys. In Bosnia around 2001, UN police monitors and employees of a US contractor bought women and girls who had been trafficked. In the United States and Australia, police took over websites used to share abuse images and kept them running for weeks or months to identify the users. Investigations found no evidence that MI5 used the Kincora boys' home in Belfast for blackmail, and the ring of powerful men that London police investigated in Operation Midland was invented by Carl Beech, who was later jailed. The claim that Jeffrey Epstein worked for an intelligence agency has not been established.

patterns.pattern: Platforms, servers and the money behind them
patterns.role: Banks and firms fined, sued or settled
patterns.role_note: Aylo (Pornhub owner) — DOJ deferred prosecution: Deferred prosecution agreement (21 Dec 2023, Brooklyn) over unlawful monetary transactions involving sex-trafficking proceeds (GirlsDoPorn — adult victims); paid over $1.8m plus victim compensation
patterns.pattern_summary: Online abuse of children depends on ordinary businesses: companies that host websites, apps and social platforms, payment services and banks. In 2025 the Internet Watch Foundation, a British charity that finds and removes abuse images, found most of the material it removed on servers in Bulgaria, the United States, the Netherlands, Romania and France. Reports of suspected abuse to the US CyberTipline, most of them made by American technology companies, rose from 4,560 in 1998 to more than 36 million in 2023, then fell to about 20.5 million in 2024; the centre that runs it attributed part of the fall to Meta encrypting its messages. Money for watching abuse streamed live flows from Australia, Britain, the United States and other wealthy countries to the Philippines. In 2020 the Australian bank Westpac agreed to pay a A$1.3 billion penalty for breaches of money-laundering law that included failing to check payments that could be linked to child exploitation. The classified advertising site Backpage earned more than $500 million from advertisements, including ones used to sell children, before US authorities shut it down in 2018.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: Indian Residential Schools — Truth and Reconciliation Commission and abuse claims; Mount Cashel Orphanage, St John's — Hughes Royal Commission; Cornwall Public Inquiry — institutional responses to historical abuse; Ontario training schools class action (Brown v. Ontario); Duplessis Orphans (Quebec) — healthy orphans falsely certified mentally ill and confined; Law Commission of Canada — 'Restoring Dignity': child abuse in Canadian institutions (2000); Childs Play — run by Australia's Task Force Argos for 11 months; Project Spade — Azov Films, Toronto; Fr Johannes Rivoire — Oblate in Nunavut, never extradited from France; Mount Cashel Orphanage — Hughes Royal Commission; Indian Residential Schools run by Catholic entities — TRC and papal apology; Canada residential schools run by Anglican, United and Presbyterian churches.
patterns.pattern_summary: In 275 cases on this map, police officers, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part in the abuse, or a court or inquiry found that they ignored, concealed or obstructed it. In Rotherham, in the north of England, an independent inquiry in 2014 estimated that about 1,400 children had been sexually exploited between 1997 and 2013 and called the failures of the council and the police "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. In Australia in 1972, a senior police officer offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. In North Wales, the police investigated allegations against their own officers. In Mexico, after the journalist Lydia Cacho exposed an abuse ring in Cancún, Puebla state police arrested her in 2005, and leaked phone calls recorded the state governor discussing her detention; he was arrested in 2021 on torture charges.

cases.title: Project Spade — Azov Films, Toronto
cases.who: Azov Films (Toronto distributor of 'naturist' films of children)
cases.what: Toronto police undercover officers made contact with a man sharing graphic abuse images in October 2010, which led to Azov Films, a Toronto company run by Brian Way that produced and sold films of child exploitation worldwide; after a joint investigation with the US Postal Inspection Service, police raided the business. Police said it was a $4 million business distributing to over 50 countries and seized over 45 terabytes of data. On 14 November 2013 Toronto police announced 348 arrests and 386 children rescued; those arrested included 40 school teachers, nine doctors and nurses, six law enforcement personnel, nine pastors and priests and three foster parents. Way was arrested in 2011 and in 2016 was found guilty of making and distributing child sexual abuse material and sentenced to ten years, reduced after a judge found he had been abused in jail.
cases.cover_up: Germany's BKA received the customer list in October 2011 but began investigating only in October 2012; a German MP on the list later resigned, and information about the case was passed to his party leader.

cases.title: Fr Paul Moore — moved by his bishop to Toronto
cases.who: Diocese of Galloway; Bishop Maurice Taylor
cases.what: Fr Francis 'Paul' Moore was found guilty at the High Court in Glasgow in 2018 of abusing three boys in Ayrshire in the 1970s and indecently assaulting a student priest in 1995, and was jailed for nine years. He had confessed his attraction to boys to Bishop Maurice Taylor of Galloway in 1996; Taylor sent him to a treatment centre in Toronto and to Fort Augustus Abbey, removed him from ministry but let him live in a church-bought house, and did not report him.
cases.cover_up: Bishop Maurice Taylor sent Moore to Toronto and Fort Augustus

cases.title: Lev Tahor — leaders convicted of kidnapping children
cases.who: Lev Tahor (ultra-Orthodox sect)
cases.what: In December 2018 Lev Tahor leaders Nachman Helbrans and Mayer Rosner took a 14-year-old girl and her 12-year-old brother in the night from their mother's home in upstate New York and moved them through several states to Mexico, where the girl was returned to the adult man the group had 'married' her to religiously at 13. The mother had fled the group's Guatemala compound in November 2018 and been granted sole custody. Both children were recovered in Mexico after three weeks. A federal jury convicted the two men in November 2021, and on 31 March 2022 each was sentenced to 12 years. Founder Shlomo Helbrans had been convicted in New York in 1994 of kidnapping a 13-year-old boy.

cases.title: Bountiful, B.C. — parents convicted of taking 13-year-old to marry Warren Jeffs
cases.who: FLDS, Bountiful community
cases.what: In February 2017 a B.C. Supreme Court judge in Cranbrook convicted Brandon James Blackmore and Emily Gail Blackmore of removing a child from Canada for sexual purposes: in 2004 they took their 13-year-old daughter to the Utah–Arizona line to be married to Warren Jeffs, then 48. Both were jailed in August 2017. In the same trial James Oler was acquitted of a related charge.

cases.title: James Oler — removing a 15-year-old from Canada to marry
cases.who: FLDS, Bountiful community
cases.what: Former FLDS Bountiful bishop James Oler was first acquitted in 2017; the B.C. Court of Appeal ordered a new trial. In May 2019 he was found guilty of removing a child from Canada, having taken a 15-year-old girl to the United States in 2004 to be married to an older FLDS member. On 29 August 2019 he was sentenced to 12 months in jail and 18 months' probation. Separately, Oler (5 wives) and Winston Blackmore (24 wives, 1990–2014) were convicted of polygamy in July 2017.

cases.title: Welcome to Video — darknet CSAM site run from South Korea
cases.who: Welcome to Video (operator Son Jong-woo / Son Jung-woo)
cases.what: A Korean-run darknet site that sold access to child sexual abuse videos for Bitcoin; it held over 250,000 unique videos and its server had more than one million Bitcoin addresses, one per account. IRS-CI tracing of Bitcoin transactions located the server in South Korea, and the operator, Son Jong-woo, was arrested on 5 March 2018. On 16 October 2019 the US DOJ announced 337 users arrested and charged, with leads sent to 38 countries (Korean police counted 310 arrests in 32 countries, 223 of them Koreans). He served 18 months in South Korea; on 6 July 2020 the Seoul High Court refused US extradition, and in July 2022 he received a further 24 months for concealing proceeds. DOJ said 45% of the videos analysed had not been known before.
cases.cover_up: South Korean courts gave the operator 18 months on appeal (May 2019); Seoul High Court refused US extradition on 6 July 2020.

cases.title: Dreamboard / Operation Delego
cases.who: Dreamboard (invitation-only bulletin board, about 600 members)
cases.what: An invitation-only bulletin board, used by an estimated 600 people, whose applicants had to upload abuse material of children aged 12 or under and keep uploading to stay. NBC reported the computers hosting the site were in Georgia, US, and the top administrators were in France and Canada. In August 2011 Attorney General Eric Holder and DHS Secretary Janet Napolitano announced charges against 72 people, with arrests on five continents including 43 in the US. By January 2013, 57 had been arrested, 45 had pleaded guilty and one was convicted at trial; 42 had been sentenced to between 10 years and life. Fifteen were known only by online identities. DOJ said at least 38 children were being abused by group members.

cases.title: Childs Play — run by Australia's Task Force Argos for 11 months
cases.who: Childs Play (Tor forum; owner Benjamin Faulkner, convicted)
cases.what: Childs Play launched on Tor on 15 April 2016 and, with over a million registered profiles, was described as the largest site of its kind. Its Canadian administrator, Benjamin Faulkner, was arrested in Virginia in early October 2016 with American Patrick Falte; in September 2017 a federal judge in Virginia sentenced both to life for sexually abusing a toddler, and in August 2019 both received 35 years for running a child exploitation enterprise on the related Giftbox Exchange site. Australia's Task Force Argos then ran Childs Play for 11 months, until September 2017, as part of Operation Artemis, to identify victims and offenders.
cases.cover_up: Queensland Police Task Force Argos operated the site for about 11 months (2016–2017), impersonating the owner and posting abuse images to keep users' trust; a UNICEF Norway legal adviser and Amnesty International criticised this, ECPAT supported it, and a York University criminologist called the server move to Australia 'jurisdiction shopping'.

cases.title: Boystown darknet platform
cases.who: Boystown (Tor platform, about 400,000 registered users)
cases.what: Boystown launched in June 2019, focused on the abuse of boys, and had 400,000 registered users when a BKA-led taskforce with Europol, the Netherlands, Sweden, Australia, Canada and the US took it down in April 2021. Three German administrators were arrested in Germany and one German national in Paraguay. In December 2022 they were sentenced to between 7 and 12 years, two with preventive detention. Successor platforms with a common German administrator were shut down around Christmas 2022.

cases.title: 764 network — founder sentenced to 80 years
cases.who: 764 (online network on Discord/Telegram; founder Bradley Cadenhead)
cases.what: 764, named after the first digits of the ZIP code of Stephenville, Texas, extorted minors into producing abuse material, self-harm and animal cruelty. Its founder, Bradley Cadenhead, was arrested in August 2021 aged 16 and on 16 May 2023 was sentenced in Texas to 80 years after pleading guilty to nine counts of possession/promotion of child sexual abuse material. The US DOJ describes 764 as a nihilistic violent extremist network and its Counterterrorism Section prosecutes it; on 29 April 2025 DOJ announced the arrests of two alleged leaders of the subgroup '764 Inferno', in North Carolina and in Greece. On 10 December 2025 Canada became the first country to list 764 as a terrorist entity.

cases.title: Landslide Productions / Operations Avalanche and Ore
cases.who: Landslide Productions (payment portal, Thomas and Janice Reedy)
cases.what: Landslide, a Fort Worth, Texas portal run by Thomas and Janice Reedy, processed credit-card sign-ups for third-party sites, some offering child abuse images. US agents raided it in August 1999; a jury convicted Thomas Reedy, who was sentenced to 1,335 years (reduced to 180 on appeal), and Janice Reedy got 14 years. US Operation Avalanche examined about 35,000 names on the database, and the FBI passed details of 7,272 British residents to UK police, starting Operation Ore, Britain's biggest computer crime investigation; raids began in May 2002. CEOP said 140 children had been rescued in the UK. Later forensic examination showed large-scale credit card fraud in Landslide's records (54,348 sets of stolen card details), and some people were wrongly accused; a legal challenge in 2009 argued that many convictions for incitement rested on flawed credit-card evidence. Follow-on operations took place in other countries.
cases.cover_up: Later reconstruction of the Landslide data found many listed names were victims of credit-card fraud, and the validity of UK Operation Ore procedures was questioned; an estimated 33 suicides followed in the UK.

cases.title: Basilian Fathers — Canadian convictions
cases.who: Congregation of St. Basil (Basilian Fathers)
cases.what: Basilian priest William Hodgson Marshall pleaded guilty in 2011 to 16 counts of indecent assault and one of sexual assault from 1952–1986 in Windsor, Toronto and Sudbury schools. Robert Whyte pleaded guilty in 1990 to abusing 18 children (1962–1982); Kenneth O'Keefe received house arrest in 2012–2013. In April 2020 the Supreme Court of Canada let stand an award of over $2.5 million, including $500,000 punitive damages, against the Basilians.

cases.title: Fr Eric Dejaeger — Oblate in Nunavut
cases.who: Missionary Oblates of Mary Immaculate; Belgian-born Fr Eric Dejaeger
cases.what: Belgian-born Oblate missionary Eric Dejaeger had served a five-year sentence in the early 1990s for 11 counts of sexual and indecent assault against children in Baker Lake, Nunavut. When charged over Igloolik he fled to Belgium, where he lived in Oblate homes for 16 years despite an international warrant; Oblate officials acknowledged they knew he was about to leave. Returned to Canada in 2011, he was convicted on 12 September 2014 of 24 further counts, and with eight guilty pleas was sentenced in 2015 for 32 sex crimes against Inuit children in Igloolik between 1978 and 1982. He received 19 years (eight after time served); appeals were dismissed in 2018.

cases.title: British child migration programmes — IICSA
cases.who: UK government; Fairbridge Society, Barnardo's, Sisters of Nazareth, Catholic Church agencies and others; receiving institutions incl. Christian Brothers
cases.what: IICSA's report of 1 March 2018 found that the child migration programmes were 'a deeply flawed government policy' and that successive UK governments failed to ensure protections against abuse. It found a catalogue of evidence that migrated children suffered ill-treatment and abuse including sexual abuse; Barnardo's suspended migration after sexual abuse came to light at its Picton school, and the Fairbridge Society failed to respond to allegations at its schools in Canada and Australia. It recommended an immediate financial redress scheme for surviving child migrants.
cases.cover_up: Successive governments continued the policy despite years of evidence that children were suffering, including sexual abuse. Fairbridge failed to respond properly to a series of sexual abuse allegations at its schools.

cases.title: Fr Johannes Rivoire — Oblate in Nunavut, never extradited from France
cases.who: Oblates of Mary Immaculate (OMI Lacombe Canada; Oblates of France)
cases.what: French Oblate Johannes Rivoire worked in the Canadian North from 1959 to 1993. He faced at least three sexual-abuse charges (1998 warrant) concerning Inuit children in Arviat, Rankin Inlet and Naujaat, and a 2022 warrant for indecent assault on a girl in Arviat and Whale Cove between 1974 and 1979. A March 2024 review by retired Quebec justice André Denis, commissioned by the Oblates, concluded on the preponderance of evidence that he assaulted six children. Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami called his death without trial in April 2024 'a systemic failure of nation states and religious institutions'.
cases.cover_up: He left for France in January 1993; a Canadian arrest warrant followed in 1998 and charges were later stayed. A 2022 warrant led to an extradition request that French authorities denied. The 2024 Denis review found the RCMP never contacted the Oblates when charges were laid. In February 2024 the Vatican ruled against his dismissal. He died in France in 2024 without trial.

cases.title: Mount Cashel Orphanage, St John's — Hughes Royal Commission
cases.who: Mount Cashel Orphanage run by the Irish Christian Brothers, with privileged foster-home status from Newfoundland Social Services; Royal Newfoundland Constabulary; provincial Department of Justice
cases.what: Complaints of abuse at Mount Cashel surfaced in 1974 and 1975 but neither led to charges. Police reopened the case in February 1989; nine Christian Brothers were convicted. The Hughes Royal Commission (156 hearing days, over 200 witnesses, report 31 May 1991) found neither the police nor the Justice Department handled the 1975–76 files normally, and that child welfare director Frank Simms insisted on special treatment for the Brothers. The province paid $11 million to more than 40 victims in 1997.
cases.cover_up: In December 1975 the police chief and assistant chief ordered Detective Robert Hillier to end his investigation after two Brothers admitted molestation; references to sexual assault were removed and the first report destroyed. The Justice Department laid no charges, and four Brothers were moved out of the province instead.

cases.title: Cornwall Public Inquiry — institutional responses to historical abuse
cases.who: Cornwall Community Police Service, Ontario Provincial Police (Project Truth), local probation office, Roman Catholic Diocese of Alexandria-Cornwall
cases.what: The Cornwall Public Inquiry under Commissioner G. Normand Glaude reported in December 2009 at a cost of over $50 million. It found systemic failures by police, probation and the Catholic diocese in responding to historical sexual abuse allegations against adults in positions of trust in Cornwall. On the long-rumoured paedophile 'clan', Glaude made no finding, saying no investigation had provided conclusive evidence.
cases.cover_up: Commissioner Glaude found the Diocese's $32,000 settlement with complainant David Silmser contained an illegal clause, and called Cornwall police's investigation of his complaint 'deeply flawed', though he found no conspiracy between police and diocese.

cases.title: Law Commission of Canada — 'Restoring Dignity': child abuse in Canadian institutions (2000)
cases.who: Government-run and government-funded institutions for children, including Indian residential schools
cases.what: In November 1997 the federal Minister of Justice asked the Law Commission of Canada to report on processes for dealing with physical and sexual abuse of children in government-run, government-funded and government-sponsored institutions. Its report, Restoring Dignity: Responding to Child Abuse in Canadian Institutions, was presented in March 2000. It reviewed the history of residential schools and other institutions and assessed redress options, recommending programmes negotiated with survivors that avoid causing further harm, together with public education and prevention measures.

cases.title: Nova Scotia — Kaufman review of the response to institutional abuse (2002)
cases.who: Nova Scotia provincial youth institutions and the province's compensation programme
cases.what: Retired judge Fred Kaufman, asked by Nova Scotia's government in November 1999 to review its response, delivered 'Searching for Justice: An Independent Review of Nova Scotia's Response to Reports of Institutional Abuse' to Justice Minister Michael Baker on 31 January 2002. The province's compensation programme for people abused in provincial youth institutions, expected to draw about 300 claims, had received 1,264 by the time it closed in 2000 and paid about $39 million in compensation and counselling. Kaufman stated that sexual and physical abuse did occur, but found the programme 'seriously flawed', found significant evidence of false and exaggerated claims, and found that employees were branded as abusers without recourse. He made 105 recommendations.

cases.title: Quebec National Assembly special commission on the sexual exploitation of minors (2020)
cases.who: Pimping networks and sex-trade establishments exploiting minors in Quebec
cases.what: A cross-party special commission of Quebec's National Assembly studied the sexual exploitation of minors for 18 months, with hearings in Quebec City, Montreal and Val-d'Or, and tabled its final report on 3 December 2020. It estimated about 600 establishments in Quebec, such as strip clubs, massage parlours and escort agencies, where a man could find a teenager for sex, described Montreal as a national hub, and said pimps could earn up to $300,000 a year. It made 58 recommendations, the first being to make the fight against sexual exploitation of minors a national priority.

cases.title: Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry — child migrants sent from Scotland (Case Study 8)
cases.who: Charities, religious orders and governments that ran child migration schemes from Scotland to Canada and Australia
cases.what: Lady Smith published the first volume of findings on child migration on 21 March 2023 and a second volume in September 2023. She found that many thousands of children were sent from Scotland, mainly to Canada and later Australia, and that some were sexually abused at their destinations, including by men in holy orders and by members of a paedophile ring. About 80,000 children were sent from the UK to Canada by 1920 and about 7,000 to Australia between 1912 and 1970; 45 people gave evidence.

cases.title: Canada — police-reported trafficking 2013–2023 (Ontario hub)
cases.who: Mostly domestic traffickers known to victims
cases.what: Statistics Canada reported on 1 November 2024 that police recorded 4,543 trafficking incidents from 2013 to 2023; about 23% of 3,558 victims were under 18 and 93% were women and girls. Ontario accounted for roughly two-thirds of incidents and Toronto alone for 20%. 91% of victims knew their trafficker and 34% were trafficked by an intimate partner; only 10% of completed adult court cases with a trafficking charge ended in a guilty decision.

cases.title: Winter Commission — Archdiocese of St. John's
cases.who: Roman Catholic Archdiocese of St. John's; Archbishop Alphonsus Penney
cases.what: Archbishop Alphonsus Penney commissioned former Lieutenant Governor Gordon Winter in May 1989 to inquire into sexual abuse of children by clergy of the archdiocese. The 1990 report assigned Penney part of the blame for covering up abuse, and he resigned after its release.
cases.cover_up: Report assigned Archbishop Penney part of the blame for covering up abuse

cases.title: Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry — Fort Augustus Abbey and Carlekemp (Benedictines)
cases.who: English Benedictine Congregation — Fort Augustus Abbey School and Carlekemp Priory School
cases.what: On 11 August 2021 Lady Smith published the Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry's findings on residential care run by the Benedictine monks of Fort Augustus Abbey between 1948 and 1991, concluding that children at Carlekemp Priory School, North Berwick, and Fort Augustus Abbey School suffered sexual, physical and emotional abuse; 43 witnesses gave evidence in 2019. A 2013 BBC investigation had presented evidence against seven Fort Augustus monks. Denis Chrysostom Alexander, sent back to Australia after parents complained, was arrested in Sydney in 2017, returned to Scotland in January 2020, pleaded guilty in June 2021 to abusing two boys and was jailed for four years and five months. Robert MacKenzie was extradited from Canada in 2020 but the case was dropped in 2021.
cases.cover_up: Complaints to senior monks were inadequately handled; after one complaint the school did not tell police and sent the monk, Denis Chrysostom Alexander, back to Australia

flows.title: Seoul → Canada
flows.what: South Korean children sent for adoption to Canada; part of about 163,898 sent abroad 1953–2008. The 2025 Truth and Reconciliation Commission found state-enabled fraud in overseas adoptions.

flows.title: UK → Canada child migrants (Home Children)
flows.what: British child migration to Canada began in the 19th century; IICSA found the Fairbridge Society failed to respond to sexual abuse allegations at its schools in Canada.

flows.title: Czech-produced abuse images → buyers in the EU and Canada
flows.what: A Czech photographer and Swedish partner distributed images of about 70 children to customers abroad.

flows.title: Films made in Ukraine/Romania → distributed by Azov Films, Toronto
flows.what: Primary producers were in Crimea (Ukraine), Romania and Germany; the Toronto firm sold to customers in over 50 countries. Start year approximate.

flows.title: Canada → Nepal (aid-worker offender)
flows.what: A Canadian humanitarian working with street children abused boys at his home in Nepal.

flows.title: Nunavut → France: Fr Johannes Rivoire
flows.what: Rivoire left the Arctic for France in January 1993; Canadian warrants (1998, 2022) went unexecuted and France refused extradition. He died in France in 2024.

flows.title: Igloolik (Nunavut) → Belgium: Fr Eric Dejaeger (fugitive 1995–2011)
flows.what: About to be charged in 1995, the Oblate fled to Belgium; Oblate officials acknowledged knowing he was leaving, and he lived 16 years in Oblate houses despite an international warrant until returned in 2011. In 2015 he was sentenced to 19 years for 32 offences against Inuit children in Igloolik (1978–82).

flows.title: Scotland → Toronto: Fr Paul Moore
flows.what: Bishop Maurice Taylor sent Moore, later convicted (2018) of abusing three children and a student priest, to Toronto and to Fort Augustus.

flows.title: Vancouver → Long Island, New York: Fr Damian Cooper
flows.what: After a 1994 abuse admission, the Archdiocese of Vancouver sent Cooper to a Long Island diocese, where he allegedly committed 'problems of a similar nature'.

flows.title: Canada → Rome: Fr Bernard Prince
flows.what: Prince was appointed to Rome in 1991; a 1993 church letter discussed keeping him hidden in the Vatican rather than facing justice in Canada.

networks.name: South Korea's four authorised overseas adoption agencies (Holt Children's Services, Eastern Social Welfare Society, Korea Social Service, Korea Welfare Services)
networks.what: The four agencies held guardianship over children and sent them abroad under government policy; Holt sent about half (AP). The TRC (March 2025) found agencies met monthly quotas for foreign partners, falsified orphan status and swapped identities, and that the state failed to supervise them. All four were implicated in the petitions (Guardian, 2023).

networks.name: Indian Residential School system (Canada)
networks.what: Federally funded schools run by churches to assimilate First Nations, Métis and Inuit children; about 150,000 attended. Tens of thousands of claims of sexual and serious physical abuse were compensated under the 2007 settlement.

networks.name: British child migration programmes
networks.what: UK government-backed schemes run by Barnardo's, the Fairbridge Society, Catholic agencies and others that sent children to Canada, Australia, New Zealand and Southern Rhodesia; IICSA found sexual abuse and failure to protect.

networks.name: Scouting organisations (national Scout associations)
networks.what: National Scout associations; the Boy Scouts of America faced more than 82,000 sexual abuse claims in its 2020 bankruptcy and had kept internal 'ineligible volunteer' files on suspected abusers.

networks.name: Orphanage trafficking and orphanage tourism (recruitment of children into institutions for donations)
networks.what: A recurring pattern in which orphanages are set up or kept full to attract foreign donations, volunteers and tourists, recruiting children who mostly have living parents, sometimes with payments to families or forged documents. Governments and the US State Department have recognised it as trafficking, and Australia's parliament classed it as modern slavery in 2017.

networks.name: Welcome to Video
networks.what: Darknet video site paid in Bitcoin, about 1.2 million members; seized 2018. 337 arrests in 38 countries announced October 2019. Start year 2015 is not in the sources opened and is omitted from cases.

networks.name: Dreamboard
networks.what: Invitation-only board, about 600 members; 72 charged in Operation Delego (2011). Start year is approximate (investigation launched 2009).

networks.name: Boylover forum
networks.what: 'Discussion-only' forum used to make contact before sharing abuse material privately; 670 suspects, 184 arrests, 230 children safeguarded (Operation Rescue, 2011).

patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role_note: 2022: Truth Commission (CEV) final report volume 'No es un mal menor' on children in the armed conflict (2022).
patterns.pattern_summary: Governments and churches held official inquiries into child abuse in institutions at different times. Canada's Hughes inquiry into the Mount Cashel orphanage began in 1989, and Ireland's Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse ran from 1999 to 2009. In the United States, Catholic bishops commissioned a national study that was published in 2004, and state grand juries and attorneys general followed. Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and Austria began inquiries after a wave of disclosures in 2010. Australia's Royal Commission sat from 2013 to 2017, the inquiry for England and Wales ran from 2014 to 2022, and New Zealand's from 2018 to 2024. France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland reported between 2021 and 2023. Several of these studies were commissioned and paid for by the Catholic Church itself. Where an inquiry surveyed the general population instead of relying on church records, the numbers were much higher: France's commission estimated that about 216,000 people had been abused as children by priests and members of religious orders since 1950, compared with about 3,000 cases the church had identified. In Italy the only national figures come from reports the Italian bishops' conference has published about itself since 2022. Brazil's Congress held inquiries into the sexual exploitation of children that reported in 2004, 2010 and 2014. The research for this map found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in the Philippines or India; India's official findings are state-level audits of children's homes, such as the 2018 audit of 110 homes in Bihar.

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role_note: 20,864 children sent abroad 2003–2022 (Selman).
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad between 1953 and 2008. Later the main sources included Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia. In each of these, investigations found children who had been bought, taken from their families or falsely registered as orphans, and adoptions were stopped or suspended by the sending country, the receiving countries, or both. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found the state responsible for human rights violations in its overseas adoptions. Receiving countries also began to investigate: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government committee reported abuses, and China ended the practice in 2024. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.

patterns.pattern: War and the taking of children
patterns.role: Abductions and sexual violence by armed groups
patterns.role_note: Colombia — FARC-EP recruitment and use of children (JEP Macro-case 07). Colombia — sexual violence against girls by ELN, FARC dissidents, Clan del Golfo (UN verified).
patterns.pattern_summary: Armed groups have abducted, enslaved and sold children as a deliberate practice. In 2014 the group calling itself Islamic State captured Yazidi women and children in northern Iraq and sold girls as sexual slaves; a UN commission reported in 2016 that more than 3,200 women and children were still held. In 2014 Boko Haram abducted 276 schoolgirls from Chibok in north-eastern Nigeria, and 82 were still captive in 2024. The Lord's Resistance Army abducted children in Uganda and the neighbouring countries over many years; in 2021 the International Criminal Court convicted one of its commanders, Dominic Ongwen, on 61 counts, including forced marriage and sexual slavery. UN fact-finding missions found sexual violence against children by Myanmar's army and by Sudan's Rapid Support Forces, against girls as young as eight. The UN verifies and publishes these attacks country by country each year.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: Colombia — sexual violence against girls by ELN, FARC dissidents, Clan del Golfo (UN verified); Colombia — Truth Commission volume on children: 16,238 recruited; recruited girls subjected to rape, forced contraception and abortion (2022); Cartagena — 'La Madame' network exploiting girls for tourists (plea 2018); Colombia — Tren de Aragua sex trafficking of Venezuelan girls; webcam industry (US TIP 2025).
patterns.pattern_summary: In 275 cases on this map, police officers, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part in the abuse, or a court or inquiry found that they ignored, concealed or obstructed it. In Rotherham, in the north of England, an independent inquiry in 2014 estimated that about 1,400 children had been sexually exploited between 1997 and 2013 and called the failures of the council and the police "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. In Australia in 1972, a senior police officer offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. In North Wales, the police investigated allegations against their own officers. In Mexico, after the journalist Lydia Cacho exposed an abuse ring in Cancún, Puebla state police arrested her in 2005, and leaked phone calls recorded the state governor discussing her detention; he was arrested in 2021 on torture charges.

patterns.pattern: Where nobody is counting
patterns.role: No national inquiry into institutional abuse found
patterns.role_note: Archdiocese ordered to disclose files on 915 accused clergy cases to journalist Juan Pablo Barrientos within 48 hours; full compliance not achieved
patterns.pattern_summary: Most counts of child abuse and trafficking come from three sources, and each leaves large parts of the world out. The first is surveys that ask a representative sample of people about their experiences. Childlight, a research centre that combines such surveys into global estimates, had them from only 60 countries in its 2026 update, too few to represent South Asia, West and Central Africa, or the Middle East and North Africa. The second is official statistics that governments send to the UN; its 2024 global report on trafficking covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied figures for 2023. The third is reports from technology companies to the US CyberTipline; in 2025, 14 percent of its 23.4 million reports could not be assigned to any country, and North Korea had 12, a number that reflects how few people there can use American apps. The research for this map also found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.

cases.title: Medellín — US federal prosecutions of travelling offenders (10 convictions by May 2026)
cases.who: US-national travelling offenders; HSI Colombia; Alcaldía de Medellín
cases.what: BluRadio reported on 21 May 2026 that US courts, working with Colombian authorities and the Medellín mayor's office, had handed down a tenth sentence in an offensive against foreigners exploiting children in Medellín: Ramón Arellano Sandoval, 65, sentenced in Miami to 30 years for attempted sexual exploitation of a 14-year-old Medellín girl, who had entered the city 48 times in two years. On 22 January 2026 Manuel Poceiro, 69, of Miami, was sentenced to life for travelling to Colombia to exploit minors, after HSI found material involving at least five minors. In March 2024 US national Timothy Alan Livingston was found in a Medellín hotel with two minors (aged between 12 and 16, per police sources); a Colombian judge issued an arrest warrant and Interpol a blue notice (charged, at large at the time).

cases.title: Cartagena — 'La Madame' network exploiting girls for tourists (plea 2018)
cases.who: Liliana del Carmen Campos Puello ('La Madame')
cases.what: Liliana del Carmen Campos Puello ran a sex network from a Bocagrande apartment in Cartagena, supplying young women and minors to parties on yachts, in hotels and at beaches and sending women to Panama, Mexico, Miami and the Bahamas; prosecutors seized 15 ledgers of clients and payments, and a WhatsApp group listed 200 women. In 2018 she accepted charges of human trafficking and conspiracy in a plea deal and was sentenced to eight years and one month; she was released on parole in 2023. US ICE supported the investigation.
cases.cover_up: At hearings she threatened to reveal the names of politicians and powerful men she said were clients (her claim, unverified).

cases.title: Colombia — Truth Commission volume on children: 16,238 recruited; recruited girls subjected to rape, forced contraception and abortion (2022)
cases.who: FARC-EP, ELN and other guerrillas, paramilitary groups, and state security forces (recruitment and use of minors)
cases.what: Colombia's Commission for the Clarification of Truth published its volume on children and adolescents, 'No es un mal menor', in July 2022. It documented 16,238 children recruited by armed groups between 1990 and 2017 and estimated the real number at 27,101 to 40,828, and described recruitment as intentional and systematic, including use of minors by the state security forces. It found that recruited girls were forced to use contraception at an early age, forced to have abortions, and subjected to harassment, rape and sexual torture.

cases.title: Colombia — sexual violence against girls by ELN, FARC dissidents, Clan del Golfo (UN verified)
cases.who: ELN, FARC-EP dissident groups, Clan del Golfo; Colombian armed forces (2 cases 2023)
cases.what: The UN verified sexual violence against 33 girls in Colombia in 2024, by the ELN (12), FARC-EP dissident groups (12), Clan del Golfo (7) and unidentified perpetrators. In 2023 it verified 26 cases, including 2 by the Colombian armed forces.

cases.title: Netherlands — Joustra committee: state failed to stop intercountry adoption abuses; all adoptions suspended
cases.who: Dutch government (Justice ministry), licensed Dutch adoption intermediaries, intermediaries in sending countries
cases.what: The Commission of Inquiry into Intercountry Adoption, set up in 2019 and chaired by Tjibbe Joustra, reported in February 2021 after a two-year investigation that found 'serious violations' in adoptions from countries including Sri Lanka, Indonesia, Bangladesh, Brazil and Colombia between 1967 and 1997/98, and concluded the Dutch government had for decades failed to prevent abuses and protect children's rights. The government suspended all intercountry adoptions with immediate effect on 8 February 2021. About 4,000 of the children were from Sri Lanka.
cases.cover_up: The government revealed in February 2021 that its officials were aware of wrongdoing for years and had failed to intervene (BBC).

cases.title: Sweden — state inquiry into intercountry adoptions (report 2 June 2025)
cases.who: Swedish state authorities and adoption organisations
cases.what: Sweden's independent inquiry into intercountry adoptions issued its report on 2 June 2025 (nearly 1,600 pages), reviewing 65 years of adoption history and documenting numerous irregularities and illegalities of which state authorities had some knowledge. Sweden had already stopped adoptions from South Korea (AP, 2024). Sweden received 9,051 Korean children 1957–2005, and in January 1975 the Swedish ambassador urged South Korea to continue sending children after it tried to halt adoptions to Scandinavia.

cases.title: Norway — NOU 2026:7 finds illegal and unethical intercountry adoptions
cases.who: Norwegian adoption organisations; Norwegian authorities; partner orphanages and bodies in 12 countries
cases.what: A government committee appointed in 2023 presented NOU 2026:7 'Forsvarlighet, risiko og tillit' on 22 June 2026. Examining adoptions from 12 countries since the 1950s, it concluded there were illegal or unethical conditions and that the Norwegian adoption system had clear shortcomings throughout the period. Individual findings included a kidnapped child adopted to Norway, a mother told she would get money if she consented, and documents deliberately falsified; payments to orphanages or organisations were sometimes linked to the number of children adopted.
cases.cover_up: Organisations did not always tell Norwegian authorities about payments or errors; authorities kept approving adoptions after learning of risks and illegalities.

cases.title: Colombia — FARC-EP recruitment and use of children (JEP Macro-case 07)
cases.who: Former FARC-EP secretariat and commanders
cases.what: The Special Jurisdiction for Peace's Case 07 investigates the recruitment and use of children by the former FARC-EP; in August 2021 it identified a provisional universe of 18,677 unique victims and has accredited 9,854. The JEP indicted former FARC-EP commanders for war crimes including the recruitment and use of children and sexual violence against children, and has referred a former FARC member accused of reproductive violence against recruited girls to its investigation unit. Former secretariat members have publicly acknowledged responsibility.

cases.title: Operation Atlas — Virtual Global Taskforce P2P sweep
cases.who: Peer-to-peer distributors and producers
cases.what: Ten Virtual Global Taskforce members (Australia, Colombia, Netherlands, Switzerland, US HSI, Korea, New Zealand, Canada, UAE, UK) arrested 303 people suspected of distributing and producing abuse material and identified 106 victims, announced November 2015.

cases.title: Colombia — ICBF investigation of 21 substitute (foster) homes
cases.who: Instituto Colombiano de Bienestar Familiar (ICBF) substitute-home (hogar sustituto) programme
cases.what: In March 2018 the ICBF opened 21 investigations into foster homes nationwide for alleged verbal abuse, poor food and neglect and relocated 44 children and 14 adolescents, with about 3,100 homes still to review. The review followed a case in Soacha in which a man was jailed on charges of sexually abusing two girls aged 7 and 8 who were in ICBF custody in a foster home; he did not accept the charges.

cases.title: Kidflix / Operation Stream
cases.who: Kidflix (paid streaming platform, 1.8 million users 2022–2025)
cases.what: Kidflix, created in 2021, let users stream as well as download abuse videos, paying in cryptocurrency converted to tokens; 91,000 unique videos (6,288 hours) were uploaded. German and Dutch authorities seized the server on 11 March 2025, when it held about 72,000 videos. Operation Stream, led by Bavarian police with 38 countries and Europol, identified 1,393 suspects and arrested 79 during action weeks in March 2025; Europol called it the largest child sexual exploitation operation in its history.

cases.title: Colombia — 1981 ring selling Andean children abroad with forged papers
cases.who: Adoption trafficking ring
cases.what: In 1981 the New York Times (Warren Hoge) reported that Colombian authorities had uncovered a multimillion-dollar ring in which hundreds of poor Andean children were taken or bought from their mothers and sold abroad with forged papers. In 2003 Interpol issued a detention order for the manager of an uncertified Costa Rica-based adoption agency suspected of trafficking babies from Colombia in 2000–2002 (suspect, not convicted).

cases.title: Colombia — Tren de Aragua sex trafficking of Venezuelan girls; webcam industry (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Tren de Aragua; ELN; webcam studios
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says Tren de Aragua and the ELN run sex-trafficking networks in Villa del Rosario, Norte de Santander, and Tren de Aragua uses Cúcuta's transport hub to move victims to Argentina, Ecuador and Peru and operates in Bogotá, Cali, Medellín and Pereira. Traffickers recruit women and girls, mostly Colombians and displaced Venezuelans, into 'webcam modelling', an industry likely worth over $1.2 billion a year. Sex trafficking of girls is prevalent in tourist areas and extractive zones.
cases.cover_up: Two complicit officials received plea-deal sentences of 7.5 years, below the statutory minimum.

cases.title: Colombia — Constitutional Court orders Medellín archdiocese to release priests' files
cases.who: Archdiocese of Medellín; Salesian Inspectorate of San Luis Beltrán, Medellín
cases.what: In May 2019 journalist Juan Pablo Barrientos, author of 'Dejad que los niños vengan a mí', asked the Archdiocese of Medellín and the Salesians for the records of 43 priests, including complaints against them. After both refused, he filed tutela actions. On 3 March 2020 the Constitutional Court ruled that the information was semi-private and that the right to information prevailed, ordering the archdiocese to hand it over. In 2022 the Court agreed to review a further petition covering 915 priests who served in Medellín.
cases.cover_up: Both the archdiocese and the Salesian province refused journalist Juan Pablo Barrientos's 2019 request for the records of 43 priests, calling them private; the archdiocese appealed the first-instance ruling against it.

flows.title: Bogotá → United States
flows.what: US immigrant visas issued to children adopted from Bogotá, FY1994–FY2014 (peak 351 in FY1994).

flows.title: Venezuela → Colombia (displaced girls and women)
flows.what: Displaced Venezuelan women and girls exploited in sex trafficking and webcam studios; Tren de Aragua moves victims through Cúcuta.

flows.title: Cúcuta → Ecuador, Peru, Argentina (Tren de Aragua transfers)
flows.what: Tren de Aragua reportedly used Cúcuta's transport hub to move trafficking victims to Argentina, Ecuador and Peru.

flows.title: United States → Medellín (travelling offenders)
flows.what: US men travelled repeatedly to Medellín (one 48 times in two years) to exploit girls; prosecuted in Miami.

flows.title: Cartagena → Panama, Mexico, Miami, Bahamas ('La Madame' network)
flows.what: Young women sent individually abroad, coached to avoid airport scrutiny.

networks.name: Kidflix
networks.what: Paid streaming platform, 1.8 million users (2022–2025), 91,000 videos; 1,393 suspects identified, 79 arrested.

networks.name: Tren de Aragua
networks.what: Transnational criminal organization originating in Venezuela. US TIP 2025 says it operates sex-trafficking networks in Colombia, using daily-debt lodging (pagadiarios) to control victims, and has affiliated groups in Peru.

networks.name: Roman Catholic Church
networks.what: The Holy See governs about 1.3 billion Catholics. From 1922 (and 1962) canonical abuse cases were handled under strict secrecy; from 2001 they were reserved to the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith under pontifical secret, which was lifted in December 2019. National inquiries in Ireland, the US, Australia, Germany, France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Portugal, Spain and elsewhere found bishops moved accused clergy and avoided police. The UN Committee on the Rights of the Child in 2014 found practices that led to impunity.

networks.name: Lev Tahor
networks.what: Ultra-Orthodox sect of about 200–300 people founded in Israel in 1988 by Shlomo Helbrans, accused of child abuse and forced marriage of teenage girls. Leaders were convicted in the US in 2021 of kidnapping two children.

patterns.pattern: Where nobody is counting
patterns.role: No survey data on online abuse in its region
patterns.role_note: Childlight's 2026 update found Middle East and North Africa lacking representative survey data on technology-facilitated child sexual exploitation.
